job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Dana Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Hollis & Son, a small accounting practice on the high street in Ashby Green, with Mr Hollis, his son Peter and one other junior. I do bookkeeping and year-end accounts for local shops, farms and a few tradespeople, mostly from paper receipts and bank statements. I finished my accounting degree top of my class, and I'm proud I got the job within two months of graduating. I share a small flat with my younger sister Mika, and on Sundays I'm at church, then lunch at my parents' house. I'm engaged to Tom, who is an electrician, and we're hoping to marry next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I've never trusted anything that says it'll change the world overnight. At work I'd tell Mr Hollis that the clients like to see a face, and that's what we sell. At church I'd probably not mention it at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd feel secure. Our clients bring their receipts in a shoebox, and the farmer who trusts Mr Hollis will not hand his books to a screen. I've never used any of the AI tools and I'm not curious about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, learn the practice's software well and finish the chartered exams in three years. I'd keep saving £200 a month for the wedding and a deposit with Tom. I'd keep helping Mr Hollis with the year-end rush, which is where I learn the most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled and grateful. I like that my work has a rhythm, spring for tax returns, autumn for farm accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or worry in your own life would stay exactly the same even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding costs and the student loan. My parents say they'll help with the wedding, but I don't want to take too much. We also worry about my father's hours at the depot, which have been cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your week is routine screen work that even a small change could touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of it, the data entry from receipts. Mr Hollis has a machine that scans them and it's mostly fine. But even if that gets slightly better, clients still need someone to explain what the numbers mean.

I'd tell Mr Hollis clients like to see a **face**.
At church I'd probably **not mention** it.
think: I feel **secure**, because local clients trust people, not screens.
I've never used **AI tools** and am not curious.
The wedding and **loan** are my real worries.
do: Learn the practice's **software** well and pass the chartered exams.
Save **£200 a month** for the wedding and a deposit.
Help with the **year-end rush**, where I learn most.
feel: Liking the **rhythm** of the work year.

steps.text: Pass the chartered accountancy exams over three years
Save £200 a month for the wedding and a deposit
Work the year-end rush with Mr Hollis and learn the farm accounts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should be careful and keep doing what we do well. I'd tell Mr Hollis we ought to ask clients what they want before buying anything. At home I'd say the big companies are selling something, and it's not always what's best for ordinary people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I worry about the practice. If a shop owner can ask a program to do the books, Mr Hollis's clients may leave for a cheaper online service and the practice may shrink. I'm the junior, and the junior is the cost that goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hollis how we could offer something the software cannot, like home visits to farms and an annual sit-down. I'd learn the new software slowly, with Peter's help, because I'd rather be told how it works than guess. I'd also keep my savings up and say to Tom we should hold off on a bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit sad. I like the old way, with the receipts and the cup of tea with the client. I'd feel the town is changing and I'm still learning how it used to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think of a task you did last week. Which part would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The receipt entry, mostly. Last week I spent a day keying in a plumber's receipts, and a scanner reads them now. What stays is the conversation: why the tax went up, what he can claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager do differently about hiring people at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Mr Hollis would delay hiring the next junior. He's 63 and not in a rush to change. Peter would push for the new things, and I'd be in the middle.

steps.text: Suggest annual farm visits to Mr Hollis as a service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough for anyone, and no honest person should pretend otherwise. At church I'd ask for prayers for people who'll lose their work. At work I'd say we need to keep our clients close and not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd be frightened. If a machine can do my job better and cheaper, a small practice like ours is a candle in front of a floodlight. I'd also be ashamed of how little I know about the tools, since I never learned them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every pound I can, probably £350 a month, and put the wedding on hold until I know where we stand. I'd talk to Tom and our families about a shared plan, since the families have always helped each other. I'd also ask if the church or local businesses could help train people who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd not sleep well. I'd say my prayers and try to be brave, but I'd feel small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say it's the day the announcement is made. What do you tell the people close to you that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom first, and we'd sit with my parents on Sunday. My father would say we'll manage as a family, and my mother would say the wedding can wait. Tom would say his work as an electrician is hands-on, so he's safer for longer, and I'd be glad and a bit jealous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what happens to the money you owe and the money you've saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying extra on the loan and keep cash. I'd cancel the wedding venue deposit if it can be returned. And I'd go to Mr Hollis early and ask honestly how long the practice can keep me.

steps.text: Save about £350 a month and hold cash instead of paying the loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and people should use it to look after each other. At work I'd say we should plan how to keep the practice going. At church I'd say we should help the young ones find honest work, with training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel less frightened than with two years, but still worried. By 2031 I'd be 27 and maybe a mother by then. I'd want my children to grow up with a parent who's home and a family that's not afraid of the next news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my chartered exams so I have something solid. I'd try to learn the software with Peter so I'm not behind. I'd also keep saving £250 a month and maybe shift to part-time hours when children come, if the practice can manage it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steady. I'd lean on Tom and my family. I think a small town copes better than a city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your plan with 5 years instead of 2?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding would still happen but smaller, and children might come a bit later. With two years I'd freeze everything. With five I can plan to live, not only to survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you do you think sees this coming, and who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hollis doesn't see it, and he is a good man. Peter sees it better, but he doesn't talk about it. My friends at church mostly say it's all in God's hands, which is comforting and not very practical.

steps.text: Finish the chartered accountancy exams by 2029
Learn the practice software alongside Peter
Plan a smaller wedding and a later start on children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should not lose heart. At work I'd say let's keep doing good work and keep our clients. At church I'd say we should teach the young ones trades and skills that last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly at peace. By 2036 I'd be 32, married with a child or two, perhaps still with the practice or running a small one of my own. I'd learn the new tools by then, because I'd have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my exams, then do an extra certificate in tax. I'd learn one new tool at a time, slowly. And I'd save for a home with Tom, and perhaps help my younger sister Mika with her studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some sadness for how fast the world is going. I'd say I can manage when I have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you start now that you wouldn't with 2 years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather have ten years to learn slowly and keep my family close than two years to panic. I'd start with the things I'm already doing well and grow from there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At 32, what do you hope your working life looks like, and what could stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to have a small family, a steady practice and a home. What could stop me is the economy, the practice closing, or my parents falling ill and needing me. That's what life brings.

I'd say keep doing good work and **keep our clients**.
I'd say teach the young **trades** that last.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32, married, with a **child** or two.
I'd learn the tools by then, because I'd **have to**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would break the practice and my plans at the same time. What would help is time to learn, support for small firms like ours, and families and churches helping each other. I wouldn't want handouts so much as a fair chance to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say I don't want anyone to think I'm against progress. Small towns run on people who know each other, and no program has ever sat in a farm kitchen and asked how the year went. I hope that still counts for something.

headlineQuote: Small towns run on people who know each other, and no program has ever sat in a farm kitchen and asked how the year went.
portrait: Dana is a **22-year-old** bookkeeper at a small family accounting practice, top of her class, engaged and living with her sister.
She has **never used** AI tools and prefers the familiar way of working.
Traditional in outlook, she trusts **family, church and work**, and wants a fair chance over handouts.
She is calm in slow worlds, **alarmed** at two years, and plans around her wedding and future family.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario, where the small practice and her wedding plans could both fail.
whatWouldHelp: **Time** to learn, support for small firms, and community help that rewards work over handouts.
